title: Cisplatin + Etoposide

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA breaks can remain unrepaired and cancer cells may stop dividing or die. Healthy cells are also affected; the infusion or prescribed capsules deliver the same medicine by different routes.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, mouth sores or diarrhoea. Tell the nurse about faintness, rash or breathing difficulty during an infusion. If capsules are prescribed, use the exact pharmacy instructions and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Effects on fertility and harm to an unborn baby

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing; normal tissues can also be affected. Kidney protection and assessment of hearing and nerves are essential during cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report changes in urine, hearing, ringing in the ears, numbness or daily function. Tell the team about infection, unusual bruising or bleeding and any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Effects on fertility and harm to an unborn baby
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which may persist

questions.q: Why are there three treatment days?
questions.a: Etoposide is planned on three consecutive days. Usually you attend for infusions on all three. The alternative capsule plan is only used when prescribed and clearly labelled by your team.

questions.q: Are etoposide capsules the same dose as the drip?
questions.a: No. The source oral alternative has a different dose and twice-daily schedule. Your prescription and pharmacy label specify your individual dose and capsule strengths. Do not convert it yourself.

questions.q: Will I have radiotherapy or immunotherapy too?
questions.a: This guide covers Cisplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

questions.q: How long does the course last?
questions.a: The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response. The passport pages are reusable records, not a prescription for a fixed number of visits.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be assessed and treated; your team reviews benefit with the agreed clinical and scan plan.

questions.q: Why might treatment be delayed or changed?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney/liver function or symptoms may need time to recover. A dose may change to reduce lasting harm. Ask which medicine changes, why, and when it will be reviewed.

questions.q: What should I say when I call?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment day, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect information.

questions.q: Can this guide decide whether treatment is safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions need your clinical results, symptoms, previous toxicity and prescriber/pharmacy review. This guide helps you understand and discuss the plan.

phases_title: Three treatment days in a 21-day cycle
phases_note: The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response.
timeline_note: This shows one reference cycle and the order of care. It does not predict a symptom-free day or when blood counts will fall.
safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Follow your unit’s temperature threshold and emergency instructions. Sudden illness or shaking chills needs urgent advice even without a high temperature.
teachback: Can you describe which days you have treatment, whether you have etoposide capsules, how you take prevention medicines and which number to call at any hour?
consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, kidney/hearing/nerve injury, infection/bleeding, fertility and pregnancy advice, infusion versus capsule logistics, delays and dose changes, and support at home. Confirm that any additional immunotherapy or radiotherapy has its own consent discussion.
urgent_extra: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, vomiting despite medicines, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Tell staff immediately about wheeze, swelling, dizziness or faintness during an infusion. Report hearing changes, ringing in the ears, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking promptly.
purpose: Cisplatin + Etoposide is chemotherapy used for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. It aims to control the cancer and its symptoms. Ask your oncology team what benefit is realistic for you and how this option compares with other suitable treatments.
schedule_summary: Cisplatin is planned on Day 1. Etoposide is planned on Days 1–3: usually all three days by infusion, or a prescribed alternative with an infusion on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response.

day_groups.title: Day 1 in the unit
day_groups.body: Etoposide is infused over about one hour before cisplatin, which is infused over about one hour on Day 1. Extra IV fluid and electrolytes before/after cisplatin make this a longer visit. Etoposide alone is given on Days 2 and 3 unless the prescribed capsule alternative is selected. The whole visit also includes review, preparation, prevention medicines and observation.
day_groups.action: Tell staff immediately about rash, swelling, wheeze, faintness or pain near the drip.

day_groups.title: Etoposide continues
day_groups.body: Return for etoposide infusions unless the team prescribed the oral alternative. If you have capsules, follow the twice-daily pharmacy label and empty-stomach instructions.
day_groups.action: Confirm today’s anti-sickness medicines. Contact the team about a missed or vomited capsule dose.

day_groups.title: After the last treatment day
day_groups.body: Follow the written prevention and rescue plan. Multi-day antiemetic cover extends to two days after the final treatment day; the exact medicines are chosen by your team.
day_groups.action: Call for sickness despite medicines, inability to drink or reduced urine.

day_groups.title: Recovery and symptom monitoring
day_groups.body: Fatigue, low counts, infection, mouth or bowel symptoms can occur between visits. Hearing and nerve symptoms may build across cycles.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan at any time; do not wait for the next appointment.

day_groups.title: Review before the next cycle
day_groups.body: The team reviews blood counts, kidney/liver function and symptoms before deciding to continue, delay or change the plan.
day_groups.action: Bring your medicine list and symptom notes; confirm the remaining course and next review.

support.title: Preventing sickness across all treatment days
support.text: Take the written anti-sickness plan even if you feel well. The plan must cover the risk of the medicines on each of Days 1–3 and the two days after the last treatment. Ask the pharmacist to show which medicines are scheduled and which are rescue medicines.

support.title: One clear steroid plan
support.text: The anti-sickness plan may include dexamethasone. Follow the prescribed day-by-day instructions; do not add an extra steroid course or extend it yourself. Tell the team about diabetes, poor sleep or mood changes.

support.title: Fluids and kidney protection
support.text: Cisplatin needs IV fluid before and after treatment and may need magnesium/potassium replacement. Your team adapts this for your kidneys, heart and fluid balance. Ask for a personal drinking plan and call if you cannot drink or pass much urine.

support.title: If etoposide capsules are prescribed
support.text: The source alternative uses capsules on an empty stomach twice daily on Days 2 and 3. Your pharmacy label gives your individual capsule dose. Do not substitute capsules for an infusion yourself, crush/open capsules, double a missed dose or repeat a vomited dose without advice. Obtain safe handling and storage instructions.

support.title: Medicines, mouth care and infection advice
support.text: Check prescriptions, painkillers, supplements and vaccines with the oncology team. Some medicines affect kidney/hearing toxicity or etoposide exposure. Follow mouth-care advice and keep the unit’s urgent contact instructions available.

evidence.title: Evidence and your own treatment decision
evidence.intro: The exact medicines, dose, population and treatment era matter.
evidence.population: Extensive-stage SCLC; JCOG9702 specifically enrolled elderly or poor-risk patients.
evidence.interpretation: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

chronology_notes.title: Before the first dose
chronology_notes.text: Confirm the diagnosis, treatment aim, blood tests, kidney/liver function and selected etoposide route.

chronology_notes.title: During the three treatment days
chronology_notes.text: Day 1 includes both medicines; Days 2–3 continue etoposide. A split cisplatin prescription, if chosen, needs a separate checked day-by-day plan.

chronology_notes.title: Support after the last dose
chronology_notes.text: The multi-day sickness-prevention plan needs to account for two days after the last SACT day. Take only the written prescribed course.

chronology_notes.title: Across and after the course
chronology_notes.text: Counts, kidneys, hearing and nerves need review throughout treatment. Some problems can persist after the final dose.

sections.title: Before each visit
sections.text: Confirm transport for Days 1–3, blood-test arrangements, prescriptions and the 24-hour contact details. Tell the team if you are ill before travelling.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Etoposide is infused over about one hour before cisplatin, which is infused over about one hour on Day 1. Extra IV fluid and electrolytes before/after cisplatin make this a longer visit. Etoposide alone is given on Days 2 and 3 unless the prescribed capsule alternative is selected. The whole visit also includes review, preparation, prevention medicines and observation.

sections.title: Infusion access
sections.text: Treatment may use a cannula or an existing suitable central line. Ask for line-care instructions if you have a line. There is no routine take-home infusion pump.

sections.title: Capsules and home medicines
sections.text: If prescribed, confirm your etoposide capsule doses, empty-stomach timing, safe handling and what to do if a dose is missed or vomited. Keep prevention and rescue medicines clearly labelled.

sections.title: Support between visits
sections.text: Arrange practical help if needed and keep symptom notes. Bring questions and a current medication list to review.

anatomy: Report tinnitus or hearing change promptly; discuss existing problems before starting.
Mouth sores can affect eating or drinking. Seek advice early.
New breathlessness, wheeze or chest pain needs urgent assessment.
Report reduced urine or inability to drink; kidney tests guide treatment.
Use prescribed anti-sickness medicines; severe vomiting or diarrhoea needs advice.
Report numbness, tingling or problems with buttons, balance or walking.
Report rash, unusual bruising or bleeding. Fever or sudden illness needs urgent advice.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its aim
chapters.intro: Confirm the full plan before starting.

items.title: The treatment covered here
items.text: This guide covers Cisplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

items.title: Why two medicines?
items.text: The platinum drug damages DNA and etoposide interferes with DNA repair. Using them together attacks cell growth in different ways. Healthy cells can also be affected.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

chapters.title: Before treatment
chapters.intro: Preparation helps the team choose a suitable plan.

items.title: Tests and fitness
items.text: Blood counts, kidney and liver tests are checked before treatment. Tell the team about existing nerve/hearing problems, other medicines and any recent infection.

items.title: Route and practical arrangements
items.text: Confirm whether all three etoposide doses are infusions or whether you have capsules on Days 2 and 3. Do not substitute one route yourself.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation and contraception before treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusions. Ask for medicine-specific advice and the required contraception period.

chapters.title: Your visits and home plan
chapters.intro: Three treatment days form one cycle.

items.title: Day 1
items.text: Etoposide is infused over about one hour before cisplatin, which is infused over about one hour on Day 1. Extra IV fluid and electrolytes before/after cisplatin make this a longer visit. Etoposide alone is given on Days 2 and 3 unless the prescribed capsule alternative is selected. The whole visit also includes review, preparation, prevention medicines and observation.

items.title: Days 2 and 3
items.text: Continue etoposide by the prescribed route, with risk-appropriate anti-sickness prevention each treatment day.

items.title: The following days
items.text: Continue only the written prevention schedule and monitor symptoms. The two days after the final treatment day are part of the multi-day antiemetic review.

chapters.title: Effects to discuss and monitor
chapters.intro: Report problems early; they are not a measure of benefit.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines may lower blood counts. Infection can become serious quickly; follow the urgent advice plan for fever, chills or sudden illness.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Platinum medicines may affect hearing, nerves and kidneys, and some changes can last. Tell the team promptly about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or reduced urine.

items.title: Mouth, bowel, hair and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness, nausea, bowel changes, hair loss and tiredness can affect daily life. Ask for help with symptoms; call urgently if you cannot drink or symptoms are severe.

items.title: Later effects
items.text: Etoposide can be associated with a later blood cancer. Discuss serious and lasting risks together with likely benefit and alternatives.

chapters.title: When to seek urgent help
chapters.intro: Use your unit’s 24-hour number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, vomiting despite medicines, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Tell staff immediately about wheeze, swelling, dizziness or faintness during an infusion. Report hearing changes, ringing in the ears, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking promptly.

items.title: When calling
items.text: Give your regimen, last treatment day and symptoms. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not wait for the next appointment or for a high temperature if you feel very unwell.

chapters.title: Review and the next plan
chapters.intro: Completion and follow-up depend on the treatment aim and response.

items.title: Course review
items.text: The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response.

items.title: Disease assessment
items.text: Scans and other assessments are arranged by the consultant. Symptoms alone do not show whether treatment is working.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Review ongoing kidney, hearing, nerve and blood-count problems. Confirm which support medicines finish and agree follow-up. Any next treatment, including immunotherapy or radiotherapy, needs a separate plan.
